title: Attention: what does "it" refer to?
objective: Learners see how attention lets a language model work out which other words matter to each word, using a sentence where changing the last word changes what "it" refers to.

recommended.why: Arcs from one focus word to every other word, thick where attention is strong, make the "it" to "cat" (or "road") link easy to see and to feel flip.

alternative.why: Arcs from one word versus the full matrix: which builds intuition, and which shows the whole picture?

assumptions: Attention weights are illustrative, made from hand-set scores passed through a softmax per row, not taken from a real model
Every word may look at every other word, before and after it, as in an encoder such as BERT; chat models such as GPT only look at earlier words
Each row includes the word attending to itself and adds up to 100%
Real models run many heads in each of many layers; two heads are shown to make the point that heads specialise
units: attention weight: percent of the focus word's attention (each row sums to 100%)
checkDescription: Every row of every attention matrix sums to 1; the meaning head's strongest link from "it" is "cat" with "tired" and "road" with "wide"; the position head's strongest link from every word is a neighbouring word.

learnerPrompts.predict: Before you switch the last word to "wide": which word do you expect "it" to attend to most, and roughly how much?
learnerPrompts.explain: Switch to the position head. Why does changing "tired" to "wide" no longer change anything, and why would a model still want a head like this?
